chapters.title: Recall drill
chapters.blurb: One recall card, then a boss.

challenges.prompt: What does a cache give up in exchange for speed?
challenges.answer: Freshness: a cached copy can be out of date.
challenges.explain: A cache serves a copy, and the copy can lag behind the source. Say how stale is acceptable.

challenges.prompt: Name one way to keep a cache fresh.
challenges.answer: Give every entry a time to live.
challenges.explain: A time to live bounds how stale an entry can get.

challenges.prompt: Which of these keep data in memory?
challenges.explain: Redis and Memcached hold data in memory, which is why they are fast and why they are caches.

challenges.prompt: Name an in-memory store.
challenges.explain: Redis keeps its data in memory.

chapters.title: Duel drill
chapters.blurb: One trade-off duel, then a boss.

challenges.prompt: Reads are slow and the same rows are read again and again. What do you add?
choices: A cache in front of the database
costs: A copy that can be stale
challenges.explain: A cache serves repeated reads from memory. The cost is a copy that can lag behind the database.

challenges.prompt: What does a cache cost you?
challenges.explain: The copy can be stale.

chapters.title: Write drill
chapters.blurb: One written answer, then a boss.

challenges.prompt: Write two non-functional requirements for a photo app.
challenges.model: About ten million uploads a day; a photo loads in under 200 ms for 99% of requests.
challenges.explain: Numbers turn wishes into decisions. Give the scale and a latency target.

challenges.prompt: What does a non-functional requirement carry?
challenges.explain: A number makes it testable.

chapters.title: Estimate drill
chapters.blurb: One estimate with a fixed answer, then a boss.

challenges.prompt: Size the busiest second.
challenges.explain: Divide a day's requests by about 100,000 seconds, then multiply by 10 for the peak.

challenges.prompt: About how many seconds are in a day?
challenges.explain: 86,400, rounded up.

chapters.title: Fill drill
chapters.blurb: One diagram to fill, then a boss.

challenges.prompt: Fill in the two empty boxes.
challenges.explain: Traffic meets a load balancer first; the rows live in the database.

challenges.prompt: What spreads traffic across servers?
challenges.explain: It spreads requests across servers.

chapters.title: Sticker drill
chapters.blurb: One diagram to sticker, then a boss.

challenges.prompt: Put each job on the box that should do it.
challenges.explain: The gateway checks who is calling; the database stores the rows.

challenges.prompt: Which box checks the access token?
challenges.explain: It is the front door.

chapters.title: Flaw drill
chapters.blurb: One flaw to spot, then a boss.

challenges.prompt: Find the weak box, then pick the fix.
fixes: Add a replica that can take over
Put a cache in front of the app servers
challenges.explain: One database with no copy is a single point of failure. A replica can take over.

challenges.prompt: What removes a single point of failure?
challenges.answer: A second copy that can take over.
challenges.explain: Redundancy.

challenges.prompt: Put the steps of a design round in order.
challenges.explain: Requirements first, because every later box has to serve one.

challenges.prompt: What comes first in a design round?
challenges.explain: Everything else serves them.

chapters.title: A full run
chapters.blurb: A miss, a second chance, a boss and the results.

challenges.prompt: Which of these are message queues?
challenges.explain: Kafka and SQS hold messages until a consumer takes them.

challenges.prompt: What does a queue smooth out?
challenges.explain: Producers can run ahead of consumers for a while.

challenges.prompt: Orders arrive in bursts and the payment service is slow. What do you add?
costs: Orders are confirmed a little later
Every order is lost on restart
challenges.explain: A queue lets orders pile up safely while payments catch up. The cost is a short delay.

chapters.title: Key points drill
chapters.blurb: A recall scored from key points, then a boss.

challenges.prompt: Why put a cache in front of a database?
challenges.answer: Repeat reads come from memory, so they are faster and the database does less work, at the price of a copy that can be stale.
challenges.principle: A cache trades freshness for speed and load.
key_points: Reads come from memory, so they are faster
challenges.explain: A cache serves repeat reads from memory. The cost is a copy that can lag behind the database.

challenges.prompt: Name one way to keep a cache fresh.
key_points: A time to live bounds how stale it gets
Update or delete it when the source changes
challenges.explain: A time to live bounds how stale an entry can get.

chapters.title: Tall feedback drill
chapters.blurb: One long list to put in order, so its feedback is taller than half a phone screen.

challenges.prompt: Put the steps of a design round in order.
items: Ask what the product must do
Pin down the numbers: users, reads, writes
Go deep on the hottest path
Say what you would build next
challenges.explain: Requirements come first, because every box later has to serve one. The numbers decide whether one machine will do. Then the API, the boxes and the data, before any deep dive: a deep dive into the wrong design is wasted time. Close with the bottlenecks and what you would do next, so the interviewer hears you weigh trade-offs, and sees where the design is weakest.

challenges.prompt: What comes first in a design round?
challenges.explain: Everything else serves them.
